claims.text: Austenitic stainless steels are used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
Increasing chromium content promotes rapid formation and stabilization of a continuous Cr2O3-rich passive film.
Increasing molybdenum content promotes rapid formation and stabilization of the passive film.
Molybdenum becomes enriched at the metal/oxide interface.
Interfacial molybdenum facilitates prompt passive-film repair after damage.
The proposed passive film minimizes localized pitting.
The proposed passive film minimizes general corrosion.
A Cr2O3-rich film acts as a barrier to corrosive species.
Molybdenum maintains passive-film integrity by enabling rapid repassivation after local disruption.
Steels with increased chromium and molybdenum will develop thicker passive films than lower-alloyed baseline steels.
Steels with increased chromium and molybdenum will develop more adherent passive films than lower-alloyed baseline steels.
Steels with increased chromium and molybdenum will exhibit lower corrosion-current densities than lower-alloyed baseline steels.
Steels with increased chromium and molybdenum will exhibit higher electrochemical impedance than lower-alloyed baseline steels.
A chloride-containing acidic aqueous environment at 80°C simulates relevant chemical-processing service conditions.
The hypothesized improvement should occur in austenitic stainless steels exposed to chloride-containing acidic environments at approximately 80°C.
Improved corrosion resistance should manifest once chromium exceeds approximately 16%.
Improved corrosion resistance requires molybdenum to be within a range sufficient to support passive-film stability.
Prior literature supports the roles of chromium and molybdenum in passive-film formation.
Microstructural and environmental variations may affect corrosion behavior independently of composition.
A controlled comparison should vary only chromium and molybdenum while holding processing and microstructure constant.
